turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. Chat. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. Chat. Um... well, I'm here because I just can't seem to keep things straight anymore. You know, organize all the moving parts of my life. I'm a software developer, but I also do a lot of other things. Like, right now I have all these patent notes to review, and I'm supposed to be prepping for this workshop... actually, the workshop is in Chicago next month. Have you been to Chicago? I went there a few years ago for a conference and the pizza was amazing. Deep dish, you know? Anyway, there's also gallery deadlines and team decisions I need to make, and it's just... a lot. Instead of prioritizing what actually matters, I just end up starting whatever is loudest, whatever is right in front of my face. Like yesterday, I spent three hours researching a new espresso machine instead of finishing a project brief. I just... I can't seem to get it together.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot organize the moving parts of their life and struggle to prioritize tasks, instead starting whatever is 'loudest'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes getting easily sidetracked by unrelated thoughts or stimuli, such as spending three hours researching an espresso machine instead of working on a project brief, and going on a tangent about Chicago pizza.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had trouble with organization and focus since childhood?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, actually, looking back... it’s always been there. Even in grade school, long before I was a teenager. I remember my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright but I daydreamed too much. I’d actually finish my assignments and then just... forget to turn them in. Or I'd completely lose my homework folders. I had this one folder, it was bright neon green with a dinosaur on it—a Triceratops, I think. I loved dinosaurs. I actually went to this natural history museum last year and they had this incredible fossil exhibit. The way they articulate the bones now is so much better than when we were kids. They used to just kind of stand them straight up, but now they pose them like they're running or hunting. It's really fascinating how paleontology has evolved. But yeah, I lost that dinosaur folder constantly. My mom was always buying me new ones.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports constantly losing their homework folders since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions that teachers noted they 'daydreamed too much,' indicating distractibility by unrelated thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes being forgetful, specifically forgetting to turn in assignments after finishing them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off on a long, unrelated tangent about a natural history museum, fossil exhibits, and paleontology before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Did you also have a lot of hyperactive or impulsive behavior as a child, like fidgeting, being unable to stay seated, or blurting things out?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I was never the kid bouncing off the walls or anything. I was more the kid staring out the window. Actually, speaking of windows, I just had to get all the windows replaced in my house. It was a nightmare. The contractor said it would take three days, and it ended up taking three weeks. And the dust! There was just this fine layer of white dust on literally everything I own. I had to take my dog to doggy daycare just so he wouldn't breathe it in. He's a Golden Retriever mix, Buster. He's the best, but he sheds like crazy, so between the dog hair and the drywall dust, my vacuum basically gave up. I had to buy a new one. I got one of those cordless stick vacuums, and honestly, it's a game changer. I don't know why I didn't get one sooner. But um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being hyper. No, I wasn't really like that. Just quiet and spacey, mostly.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by going on a long tangent about home repairs and forgetting the question, and notes they were 'spacey' and 'staring out the window' as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies the doctor's question about fidgeting.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies being unable to stay seated, stating they were not bouncing off the walls.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient denies being constantly active, stating they were 'never the kid bouncing off the walls' and were 'quiet'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient denies the doctor's question about blurting things out, reiterating they were 'quiet and spacey'.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, were you already having these attention and organization problems?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, like I was saying a minute ago, it was definitely in grade school, so way before I was 12. I think I was maybe eight or nine when I had that Triceratops folder? That was right around the time my dad bought this huge station wagon with the fake wood paneling on the side. Man, those things were so ugly, but he absolutely loved it. He would spend every single Sunday morning out in the driveway washing it. He had this very specific routine with two different buckets and a special chamois cloth. 

I actually really need to get my car washed, now that I think about it. The pollen right now is just ridiculous, isn't it? It's coating everything in this thick yellow film. I must have sneezed five times just walking from the parking garage to your office today. The allergies this season are just brutal. I tried taking that over-the-counter stuff but it just makes me sleepy. Have you noticed the pollen being worse this year? 

But, uh... what did you ask? Oh, right, before age 12. Yeah, definitely. I was always losing track of my stuff back then.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they were 'always losing track of my stuff back then.'
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts (tangents about a station wagon, car washing, pollen, and allergies) to the point of forgetting the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have trouble with reading or writing, like reading slowly or making a lot of spelling mistakes?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I read pretty quickly, actually. I kind of have to for my job. I'm a software developer, so I spend half my day just reading documentation and staring at lines of code. Though, honestly, the documentation for most of these new frameworks is just absolute garbage lately. It's like nobody knows how to write a clear manual anymore. 

I was trying to integrate this new API last week for a project—we're migrating our whole database to the cloud right now, which is a massive headache. My boss wants it done by the end of the month, but he completely ignores how many legacy dependencies we have tied up in the old system. He’s one of those guys who just points at a whiteboard and expects magic. He actually wore this incredibly loud, bright pink Hawaiian shirt to our morning Zoom meeting yesterday. It had these little neon pineapples all over it. I couldn't even look at the screen, it was so distracting. I don't know where he even buys something like that... probably from one of those targeted Instagram ads. I get so many of those lately, mostly for really expensive coffee gear. I actually did end up buying a burr grinder from one of them, though, and it makes a huge difference. 

But, um... wait, I'm sorry, what were you asking? Something about spelling mistakes? Oh, right. No, my reading and writing are totally fine. I don't have any issues with that.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as their boss's bright Hawaiian shirt during a Zoom meeting.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, unprompted monologue about various unrelated topics before remembering the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of reading to software documentation, their boss, his shirt, Instagram ads, and coffee grinders.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have any trouble with math in school?
turns.patient_response:
No, math was actually always my best subject. It just kind of clicked for me, you know? It's probably why I ended up in software development. Everything is just logic and patterns. I actually used to do Sudoku puzzles in the back of my history class because I was so bored. Speaking of puzzles, my wife and I started doing those massive 1,000-piece jigsaw puzzles during the pandemic, and we just never stopped. We have this one going right now that's a picture of the Neuschwanstein Castle in Germany. It's incredibly frustrating because half the puzzle is just the blue sky and these really similar-looking green trees. We had to buy one of those special felt mats so we could roll it up and put it away when we need to use the dining room table. 

We actually had some friends over for dinner last weekend, so we had to roll it up. I made this incredible beef bourguignon. I got the recipe from this French cooking channel on YouTube. The guy who runs it is hilarious, he's always yelling at the camera about using enough butter. I probably went through three whole sticks of butter just for that one meal. My cholesterol is probably screaming at me, but it was totally worth it. We paired it with this really nice Pinot Noir that we picked up on our anniversary trip to Oregon last year. 

But, uh... sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Oh, math. Right. No, math was never a problem for me. I was always pretty good at it.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by their own unrelated thoughts, drifting from math to puzzles to cooking and wine before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, rambling monologue and acknowledges this habit by saying 'I'm doing it again, aren't I?', indicating excessive talking.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often make careless mistakes when you’re doing work or other tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I definitely do that. Especially at work. Like, in code reviews, I'll miss something embarrassingly small, you know? Like a reversed condition or maybe a version number in a dependency file. And then later, when someone points it out, I can see it was right in front of me, but I just completely skimmed past it. 

Speaking of skimming, I was at the grocery store yesterday—just running in to grab some milk and bread—and I ended up standing in the magazine aisle for, like, twenty minutes just flipping through this woodworking magazine. I don't even do woodworking! But they had this whole article on building your own cedar canoe. It looked amazing. The pictures were incredible. It made me want to move to a cabin by a lake somewhere and just build boats all day. You ever think about doing something like that? Just dropping everything and moving to the woods? My buddy Dave did that a few years ago. He bought this plot of land up in Maine, completely off the grid. He grows his own vegetables now and has, like, six chickens. He sent me a picture of this massive zucchini he grew last week. It was practically the size of a baseball bat. I don't even know what you do with a zucchini that big. Make a lot of bread, I guess? My mom used to make zucchini bread when I was a kid, with those little chocolate chips in it. 

Wait, sorry. I completely lost my train of thought. You were asking about careless mistakes, right? Yeah, I definitely make those. I just miss the little details sometimes.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly confirms making careless mistakes and missing small details, such as reversed conditions or version numbers during code reviews at work.

turns.doctor_question: As a child, were you often physically restless or unable to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
As a kid? Hmm. I don't really remember being the type of kid who was bouncing off the walls or anything. But I definitely get that feeling now, especially at work. Like, on these really long design calls, I feel this intense pressure building in my body to just get up and move. I end up pacing all around my office, or I'm constantly shifting from chair to chair even when I’m trying to look focused on the webcam. 

I actually ended up buying one of those motorized standing desks recently to see if it would help. It's one of the really heavy wooden ones. The delivery guy looked like he wanted to murder me when he had to bring it up our front steps. We have these incredibly steep concrete steps because the house was built in the 1920s. It's a craftsman style, which I love, but the insulation is just an absolute nightmare. Our heating bill last January was astronomical. We tried putting that heat-shrink plastic film over the windows to keep the drafts out, but our cat just tears it down immediately. He's an orange tabby, absolute menace. He knocked a full glass of water onto my mechanical keyboard last week and completely ruined the switches. I had to order a whole new set of Cherry MX browns, which took forever to ship because of some supply chain issue. It feels like everything is just stuck on a cargo ship somewhere these days, doesn't it? I actually watched this fascinating documentary on Netflix last month about the logistics of those massive shipping containers and how they load them at the ports. The cranes they use are just engineering marvels... 

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling again. You asked about sitting still, right? So, yeah, I do get that physical pressure to move around a lot, especially during those long meetings.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, drifting from the topic of their desk to their house, cat, keyboard, and a documentary.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes constantly shifting from chair to chair, indicating squirming or fidgeting while seated.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to leaving their seat and pacing around the office during webcam calls where they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms experiencing an intense physical pressure to get up and move around, particularly during long meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, rambling monologue about various unrelated topics before catching themselves.
